passage: On the last afternoon before the zoo trip, Ganga Ma'am read out the list. Naveen looked at his big blue backpack under the desk and remembered last time: books, a toy car and two water bottles had dragged at his shoulders until his neck ached by lunch. "This time, only what I will use," he thought. At home that evening he took out the toy car, the storybook and the extra tiffin and put them back on the shelf. He chose the small red bag, put in water, lunch and a cap, and lifted it with one finger. "Easy," he said.

qa.q: What did Naveen take out of his bag?
qa.a: He took out the toy car, the storybook and the extra tiffin.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as he looked at his big backpack?
qa.a: He was wary of another aching neck like last time, so he felt determined to carry only what he would use.

qa.q: What else could Naveen do to keep his bag light and still be ready, and why?
qa.a: He could ask what the zoo provides, so he does not carry things he can get there.

qa.q: How might Ganga Ma'am see a child with a small bag on a long walking day?
qa.a: She likely sees a child who can keep up all day without tiring, whose bag holds only what he needs.

grounding: A boy remembers how a heavy bag tired him before and decides to carry only what is needed in a small bag.

subtype: Approach: keeping the bag light and taking only what is needed [Thinking]
passage: My neighbour Harsha was going on the class trip to the lake, and on the evening before, I was helping his mother fold clothes on their balcony when he came out with two bags. The big one had his whole toy car collection, three books and a board game. The small one had a water bottle and a cap. He stood there looking at both. "Last year I took the big bag to the zoo," he said, mostly to himself, "and my shoulders hurt all day and I couldn't run." He took the cars out. Then the books. He put his lunch and a jacket into the small bag. I don't know if he was sad about the cars. He looked lighter, somehow.

qa.q: What was in Harsha's big bag?
qa.a: His whole toy car collection, three books and a board game.

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling as he took the cars out?
qa.a: He may have felt a little sad to leave them but also relieved about carrying less, though the neighbour can't be sure.

qa.q: What else could Harsha do if he wants something to play with on the trip?
qa.a: He could take one small toy that fits in a pocket, so he has fun without a heavy load.

qa.q: How does Harsha's choice look to his mother?
qa.a: His mother would likely be pleased that he remembered last year and planned a lighter bag.

grounding: It shows a boy recalling that a heavy bag tired him last time and choosing to leave toys and extra books for a small bag he can carry.

passage:
Wednesday: On the zoo trip, Rafiq's backpack was so heavy that by lunchtime he was dragging it along the path. His friend Sarika raced ahead to see the tigers. Rafiq sat on a bench, shoulders aching.
The next Monday: The school sent a notice for a nature walk on Friday. Rafiq looked at his big backpack. "Last time I carried everything and saw nothing," he thought. He found his small cloth bag.
Thursday: He packed water, a cap, lunch and a notebook. He left out the comics, the torch, the extra jumper. "Enough," he said.
Friday: On the nature walk he kept up with Sarika the whole way and was the first to spot a kingfisher.

qa.q: What bird did Rafiq spot first on Friday?
How did Rafiq feel sitting on the bench at the zoo?
qa.a: He felt tired and disappointed, with aching shoulders, missing the tigers.

qa.q: What else could Rafiq do if he is unsure what to leave out?
qa.a: He could ask a teacher what the walk really needs, so he packs only what is useful.

qa.q: How does the lighter bag look to Sarika?
qa.a: Sarika finds Rafiq keeping up with her this time, so she probably enjoys having her friend beside her.

grounding: It shows a boy remembering a heavy bag tired him, then leaving toys and extra things out and choosing a small bag he can carry all day.
